newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, C Asian states have Afghan plan-Interfax.
newsitem.headline: Russia, C Asian states have Afghan plan-Interfax.

text.p: Defence ministers from Russia and three Central Asian states have worked out a joint plan of action in case the Islamic Taleban militia brought the war in Afghanistan to the country's borders, Interfax news agency said on Wednesday.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov told Interfax the conflict in Agfhanistan was threatening regional security and called for immediate joint action by the four states to try to relaunch peace efforts there.

Rodionov spoke after meeting his counterparts from Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan in the Uzbek capital Tashkent to work out joint measures in case Taleban forces seize northern Afghanistan, along the Tajik and Uzbek frontiers.

"Interfax learnt from a competent source that the meeting had worked out concrete and coordinated actions which would serve as an adequate reaction to the possibility of the military units of Taleban moving close to the southern borders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS)," the agency said.
It gave no details but quoted the defence minister of Uzbekistan as saying events in Afghanistan had caused "common alarm".

Russia, which plays a leading role in the loose 12-member CIS set up on the ashes of the Soviet Union, has deployed about 6,000 peacekeepers in Tajikistan, whose government is embroiled in a conflict with an Afghan-based Islamic opposition.

It also keeps up to 15,000 frontier guards who help patrol Tajikistan's mountain border with Afghanistan against both Islamic guerrillas and drug runners from the "Golden Crescent" narcotics producing area, which extends to Pakistan.

Russian officials have complained that the Uzbek and Kyrgyz authorities have failed to help the Tajik government. Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzia have seemed sceptical of Moscow's warnings that the advance of Afghan Islamic fundamentalists could destabilise the region.
But that situation appears to have changed somewhat after the Taleban's gains in recent months against northern Afghan warlords, some of whom are ethnic Uzbeks.
Defence analysts in Moscow say the spectre of a major influx of refugees, arms and drugs from northern Afghanistan had alarmed the leaders of three Central Asian states.
Turkmenistan, a former Soviet republic which also has a border with Afghanistan, did not attend the Tashkent talks.
